District pages that still name Jammu Tawi as Kashmir's railhead predate the June 2025 Katra–Srinagar line and are not used for rail. No prices are given.

overview.text:
Jammu and Kashmir is a union territory of two halves, north of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab and west of Ladakh. The Kashmir Valley, about 1,850 m up and walled in by the Pir Panjal, has Srinagar, its summer capital, with Dal Lake, shikaras and Mughal gardens, and the mountain resorts of Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg. The Jammu region, on the Chenab, Tawi and Ravi, has Jammu city — the winter capital and the city of temples — and Katra, the base for the Vaishno Devi pilgrimage.

Travel has changed recently. Since June 2025 trains run from Katra to Srinagar over the Chenab bridge, the highest rail arch bridge in the world, and road tunnels at Patnitop, Banihal and Z-Morh shorten the mountain roads. Security has changed too: after the April 2025 attack near Pahalgam many sites closed, and most reopened in 2026. The UK government still advises against all travel outside Jammu city, so check your own government's advice and your insurance before planning.

Beyond the famous resorts are Mughal spring gardens at Achabal, Kokernag and Verinag, the Aharbal falls, lakes such as Manasbal and Wular, and, in the Jammu hills, Patnitop, Sanasar and Bhaderwah.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Srinagar's airport is about 12 km from the city and Jammu's about 8 km.

By rail: since June 2025 trains run all the way from Katra to Srinagar across the Chenab bridge, and the Jammu–Baramulla line links the Kashmir Valley to the national network. For Amarnath, Srinagar station serves the Baltal route and Anantnag the Pahalgam route.

By road: the Jammu–Srinagar highway runs through the Patnitop (Chenani–Nashri) and Banihal–Qazigund tunnels. The Mughal Road over Peer Ki Gali links Poonch and Rajouri with Shopian but closes with winter snow. The UK FCDO advises against all travel on the Jammu–Srinagar highway.

best_time.text:
Spring: the Tulip Garden in Srinagar flowers, and much of the valley's rain falls now, not in the monsoon.

Summer: the high meadows open — Doodhpathri and Gurez are cut off by snow in winter — and July–August is the Amarnath Yatra season, with Manasbal's lotus in bloom. Jammu is very hot, with highs up to 46°C.

Winter: Gulmarg is India's best-known ski resort. Gurez is cut off for about six months when snow closes the Razdan Pass, and the Mughal Road closes with snow.

overview.text:
Srinagar, at about 1,585 m, is the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, spread around Dal Lake. Shikaras glide past carved wooden houseboats, and on the slopes above the lake the Mughal gardens — Shalimar Bagh, Nishat Bagh and Chashme Shahi — step down in terraces of lawns, fountains and water channels. The old city has the wooden Jamia Masjid, the papier-mâché-decorated Khanqah-e-Moula and bazaars full of pashmina and handicrafts.

Since June 2025 the railway has linked the Kashmir Valley with the rest of India, and Srinagar's airport has flights from Delhi, Mumbai and Jammu. Before planning a visit, check current travel advice: as of October 2026 the UK government advises against all travel to Jammu and Kashmir.

overview.text: Dal Lake covers about 18 sq km at the heart of Srinagar. Carved wooden houseboats — a legacy of British visitors, who were not allowed to own land — line its shores, and shikaras with heart-shaped paddles ferry visitors across the water and through channels to Nagin Lake. At dawn, a floating vegetable market gathers near Nehru Park. The floating gardens bloom with lotus in July and August, and in the coldest winters the lake can freeze. There is even a floating post office on a houseboat, and the white marble Hazratbal shrine stands on the shore.

overview.text: Shalimar Bagh is the largest Mughal garden in Kashmir. The emperor Jahangir laid it out in 1619, and Shah Jahan had it extended in 1630. Its 12.4 hectares descend in three terraces along a single central channel, the Shah Nahar, adapting the Persian four-part garden to the hillside. On the lowest terrace, the Diwan-e-Aam has a small black marble throne set over a waterfall. Huge chinar trees shade the lawns. Jahangir named the garden Farah Baksh, 'the delightful'; Shah Jahan's extension was called Faiz Baksh, 'the bountiful'.

overview.text:
Gulmarg lies in a cup-shaped valley of the Pir Panjal at 2,650 m, about 56 km from Srinagar; legend says Sultan Yousuf Shah named this 'meadow of flowers' in the 16th century. In winter it is India's best-known ski resort, with snowboarding, heli-skiing and tobogganing. In summer the meadows fill with wildflowers, and the golf course is among the highest anywhere.

The two-stage Gulmarg Gondola climbs from the resort to Kongdoori and on to about 3,980 m on Apharwat; the stages take roughly 9 and 12 minutes. Check current travel advice first: as of October 2026 the UK government advises against all travel to Jammu and Kashmir, including Gulmarg.

overview.text:
Sanasar is named after two small lakes, Sana and Sar, in Ramban district, 20 km west of Patnitop. At 2,050 m its meadows make it the hub for adventure sports in the Jammu region — above all paragliding — with views to the Brammah peaks.

Patnitop is next door, so the two are usually combined. A few hours' walk up the ridge is the 400-year-old Shankh Pal temple at 2,897 m, built of stone without mortar and dedicated to the serpent deity Nag Shankh Pal.

overview.text:
Mansar Lake, 62 km from Jammu in Samba district, is a forest-fringed lake that shares the sanctity of Manasarovar. A shrine to Shesha, the serpent, stands on its east bank, and temples to Shiva, Narasimha and Durga are nearby.

Surinsar Lake, 9 km away, is its twin; together they were listed as a Ramsar wetland in November 2005, with a wildlife sanctuary between them. Surinsar has a small island in the middle that is home to thousands of bats.

overview.text:
Jammu, the winter capital, spreads either side of the Tawi below the Shivaliks and is called the city of temples. The Raghunath Temple, built 1853–1860 with seven shikharas, is one of north India's largest temple complexes. Bahu Fort, 5 km from the centre, holds the Bave Wali Mata temple, busiest on Tuesdays and Sundays, above the Bagh-e-Bahu garden.

The Dogra rulers' Amar Mahal (1862) has a 120-kg gold throne, and the Pink Hall of Mubarak Mandi holds the Dogra Art Museum. Summers are very hot — up to 46°C.

overview.text:
Katra, 42 km from Jammu, is the base town for the Vaishno Devi pilgrimage on Trikuta hill. Every pilgrim must register and carry an RFID Yatra Access Card. The trek is about 14 km; helicopters and battery cars are alternatives, a ropeway runs from the Bhawan to Bhairon ji from 9 am to 5 pm, and the Shrine Board runs free langars round the clock.

Katra is also the start of the train line to Srinagar, opened in June 2025. Nearby are the Shiv Khori cave and the Siyad Baba waterfall.

overview.text:
Patnitop is a hill resort on the Jammu–Srinagar highway amid deodar and pine, and a favourite stop for Vaishno Devi pilgrims. Its winter snow used to block the highway; the 9.28-km Chenani–Nashri tunnel now bypasses it.

There is paragliding in summer, a gondola from Sanget, skiing at Natha Top in winter and the 600-year-old Naag Mandir. Sanasar's meadows are 20 km west.

Older still is the Sudh Mahadev temple, believed to be about 2,800 years old, and near Dawariyai the Billo ki Powri stairway climbs 270 steps cut into the mountain.

overview.text:
Sonamarg, 'meadow of gold', lies at 2,730 m on the Sindh, and the Z-Morh tunnel now gives it all-weather road access. Private vehicles aren't allowed on the road to Thajiwas Glacier — hire a taxi or a pony. In May 2024 part of a glacier near Thajiwas collapsed and a tourist died, so stay off unstable snow.

Treks lead to Vishansar, Krishansar, Gangabal and Gadsar lakes, and Baltal, 15 km east, is the base for the Amarnath Yatra's northern route.

items.title: Glacier
items.body: Stay off unstable snow at Thajiwas — part of a glacier collapsed in May 2024, killing a tourist.

overview.text:
Doodhpathri, 'valley of milk', is a bowl of meadows at 8,957 ft in the Pir Panjal of Budgam district, about 42 km from Srinagar. There are no permanent settlements: snow cuts it off in winter, and in summer shepherds bring their herds up to graze.

It was among the sites reopened in February 2026 after closures that followed the April 2025 attack.

overview.text:
Gurez, at about 2,400 m in Bandipora district, lies near the Line of Control; Dawar is its main town and the pyramid peak of Habba Khatoon its landmark. Heavy snow closes the Razdan Pass and cuts the valley off for about six months a year.

After closures that followed the April 2025 attack, Gurez was due to reopen in 2026 once snow cleared. Check current access and advice before going.
